A close reading for the week

“For the life of him he could not remember”

The Doves’ Nest · The Fly

A prosperous man, reminded of his son killed in the war six years ago, finds he cannot weep. He drops ink on a fly instead, and the story ends in a forgetting so complete that the reader has to carry the grief the character has lost.

He’s a plucky little devil, thought the boss, and he felt a real admiration for the fly’s courage.1 That was the way to tackle things; that was the right spirit. Never say die; it was only a question of…. But the fly had again finished its laborious task, and the boss had just time to refill his pen, to shake fair and square on the new-cleaned body yet another dark drop.2…

  1. 1

    Admiration from the man holding the pen

    The boss admires the fly’s courage in the clichés of wartime encouragement (“plucky little devil”, “the right spirit”, “never say die”), while he is the one dropping the ink. The language is that of the recruiting poster and the memorial speech. Mansfield lets the boss praise endurance in the terms a nation used for its soldiers, and be, at the same moment, the source of the ordeal.

  2. 2

    “Fair and square”

    He shakes the drop “fair and square” onto the fly, the idiom of sportsmanship applied to torment. Each blot is a test set with mock-fairness, and each time the fly cleans itself the boss sets another. The rhythm of the passage is the rhythm of the experiment: relief, admiration, ink, again. Whether the boss is God, fate, the generals, or simply a man who cannot bear his own feeling, the story does not say. It only shows the hand and the pen.
